checkpoints: A watermark is a monotonic high-water mark: a standing promise that no event will arrive earlier than `watermark - tolerance`, so it must only ever move forward in time, never backward.

In the given code, `this.watermarkMs = eventMs` runs unconditionally at the very top of `process()`, before the late-check even executes, with no guard comparing the incoming event time against the current watermark.

Because the assignment is unconditional, a back-dated event (for example one arriving two minutes in the past) drags `watermarkMs` down to its own older timestamp, dragging the watermark backward instead of leaving it at the highest event time actually seen.

Once the watermark has retreated into the past, the very next on-time event is compared against that artificially low value in `eventMs < this.watermarkMs - this.watermarkToleranceMs`, so the condition is far less likely to trip and events that are genuinely late relative to the stream's true progress start sailing through as `accepted`.

This effectively reopens a window the true watermark had already closed, and the resulting accepted/late classification becomes unstable and dependent on the exact order in which events happen to be interleaved, rather than on each event's own timestamp.

The fix is to make the watermark update conditional and move it after the late-check: only assign `this.watermarkMs = eventMs` when `eventMs > this.watermarkMs`, inside the branch that already determined the event is not late, so a late event is still classified `late` but never gets to move the watermark.

Correct behaviour can be verified by replaying an on-time -> late -> on-time sequence and asserting that the watermark value never decreases step to step, the back-dated click is reported as `late`, and the on-time clicks that follow it remain `accepted` rather than flipping to `late`.
